title: Knowledge Hiding Degrades Sense-making and Decision Quality
author: PM Researcher
summary: This piece revisits the author's earlier argument that systems thinking should precede analytical thinking, adding an important qualifier raised by a reader: the claim only holds where organizations actually let people see the whole system. Drawing on Karl Weick and a 2000 study of shared mental models, the author argues that as organizations scale, visibility into the overall strategy becomes scarce and is often deliberately hoarded by executives as a form of positional protection. The result is a workforce that executes technically well but aims at the wrong targets, because no one below the top has enough exposure to see how their work connects to the larger whole. The piece reframes knowledge hiding not as an individual failing but as a structural incentive problem baked into how large organizations distribute information. Its central move is to shift the burden from 'teach people to think in systems' to 'redesign the organization to distribute the systems view' — a much harder and more consequential ask of leadership than adopting a thinking framework.
points: Systems thinking isn't a universal skill gap — it's often an access problem: small companies naturally expose the whole system, large ones don't.
Executives frequently retain sole access to the 'systems view' not just because their role requires it but because holding it protects their position.
Talented employees plateau not from lack of ability but from never having enough exposure to see how their work fits the larger strategy.
The real fix isn't better individual thinking frameworks — it's redistributing visibility into the whole system, a harder cultural change than training.
quotes: Executives get the systems view partly because their role demands it, and partly because holding it protects their position. Almost no one below them gets to see how the pieces fit together, or where the real leverage points are, until leadership decides it's time to share.

You end up with technically excellent execution aimed at the wrong target. Talented staff can plateau because they've never had enough exposure to see how their work connects to anything outside their own lane.
Access to the systems view becomes currency, and that's not an accident; it's built into the incentive structure.

If an organization wants people who think in systems rather than just execute, it has to distribute the systems view rather than hoard it at the top. That's a much harder cultural shift than picking the right framework.

In smaller organizations, seeing a system and all its parts is usually accessible. A 15-30 person company can view the whole board of a strategy as it comes into view, including relationships with clients and users and a roadmap to the vision.
